abstract: Agricultural expansion and intensification are reducing populations of resident insectivorous birds worldwide, with potentially negative consequences for natural pest control, particularly in the tropics. Many migratory insectivores spend the non-breeding season in the tropics, often favouring disturbed habitats, potentially fulfilling ecological roles once played by resident species. However, few studies have examined the relative impacts of agricultural land-use change on resident and migratory bird species, particularly in the Afrotropics. Using field survey data from five study areas in Zambia, we examine how resident and migratory birds respond to land-use change and assess the contribution of long-distance migrants to invertivore functional diversity in human-modified landscapes. We show that, while resident invertivore richness and abundance decline, migrants are more species-rich and abundant in agricultural habitats than in forests. Trait-based analyses further reveal that migrants contribute unique functional diversity, particularly in smallholder and commercial farms, where their morphological traits overlap and extend beyond the current diversity of residents, occupying an estimated 44% of the total community morphospace in commercial farms. On one hand, our findings highlight the crucial importance of Afrotropical farmland for the conservation of migratory birds. On the other hand, the seasonal influx of migrants may have an important functional consequence, boosting the diversity and pest-predation potential of tropical bird communities. The conservation of migratory bird populations, throughout their breeding and wintering ranges, offers one route to supporting more sustainable agriculture in rapidly changing Afrotropical landscapes.
